preamble: Priya is spending the day at home with her grandad while her mum is out. He has decided to get the lawnmower out of the shed, which nobody has opened all summer.
body:
Grandad has the screwdriver in his mouth while he works at the shed bolt, which is what he does when both hands are busy and he has forgotten anybody is behind him.

"Swollen," he says round it. "Wood swells. One hot summer and every door in the country stops shutting properly."

Priya stays where she is, on the flagstone by the water butt. From here she can see the place under the roof where two boards have pulled apart, and the small traffic going in and out of it, as regular as buses. Two go in. One comes out. Her eyes do the counting now without being asked.

"Mum said leave the grass."

"Your mum says a lot of things on her way out of the door." The bolt moves half a centimetre and stops. He wipes his hands down his shirt and looks at the door the way he looks at the car when it will not start.

She found them on the second day of the holidays. Her ball had gone down the side of the shed into the nettles, and while she was reaching in, the wall began to hum against her ear, low and busy, like a machine left running in a room nobody used. She stood there a long time with the ball in her hand. After that she came out every morning before anyone was up. She put a jam jar lid of sugar water on the concrete and watched what landed on it. By the end of the week she could tell the slow heavy ones from the ones that hovered before they settled. On the Sunday she took the torch out and held it to the gap. The nest hung under the roof board, grey and layered like wet newspaper pressed into a bowl. She told nobody. There was nobody in the house who would have wanted to know, and a thing you have not told anybody stays exactly the way you left it.

"Got it," Grandad says.

The bolt comes out all at once and he staggers back a step, laughing at himself. He puts one hand flat on the door.

"Mower out, and your mum comes home to a garden she recognises."

"You don't have to."

"I do, love." He looks at her properly for the first time since they came outside. "You've gone quiet on me."

"I'm alright."

"I'm not going to lift it, if that's what's bothering you. It's got wheels on it for a reason. Your mother has me down as about ninety." He knocks twice on his hip, which is his joke, and waits for her to laugh at it.

Priya looks past his shoulder at the roofline. The traffic under the boards has changed. There are more of them out than she has ever seen at once, and they are not going anywhere in particular, only turning over the same square of air above the guttering.

"Grandad."

"Mm."

She has said his name twice this morning in that voice, and both times he has answered a different question.

He gets his fingers into the gap at the edge of the door and pulls. The wood comes away from the frame with a sound like a tooth going, and a hand's width of dark opens up. Something small comes out of it at head height and passes his ear, and he swats at the side of his face without much interest, the way you would at a fly over the sink.

Then he stops. He is listening to the door.

"Oh," he says. "Oh, hang on."

He steps back off the path. He is already turning towards the house, already working out which cupboard it is kept in, and Priya is across the flagstones with two fists in his sleeve before she has decided anything at all.

"Don't," she says. "Don't get the spray. They're mine."
